utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Defence ready to start the cross-examination of the witness once the witness has been escorted into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- oh, yes, there was one question left.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we need the witness anyhow, Ms. D'Ascoli. It's true, I've -- Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And could I also receive from the Defence an indication as to how much time the Defence would need for the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Last night we reorganised ourselves. My estimate is two hours, but I am going to address you at one point in time because the witness spoke about something new yesterday. During the night, we tried to receive additional information from Bosnia, and we tried to get this translated, so we'll see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you when we arrive at that point. By the way, in the statement, I found several times - at least two times - the word that someone was "drug in," which I understood to be that person was "dragged in" or was "dragged to." I tried to verify, but "drug in" seems not to be English. But, Mr. Groome, perhaps or --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. No, I remember that point, Your Honours. I think you're correct. Maybe I can ask the witness to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if everyone agrees that that is what apparently is meant, then there's no need to further address the matter, but ... I started doubting my own knowledge of the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Osmanovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. This morning, Ms. D'Ascoli will have one or more questions for you, and then you'll be cross-examined after that by Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can the Court Officer please call up P183. Mr. Osmanovic, I'm going to show you a photo -- photograph. Can you see the photo on the screen?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please describe what this photo depicts.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camp of Susica in Vlasenica is depicted in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I also ask the Court Officer to provide the witness with a marking pen, in red colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, please wait for my full instructions before making any markings on the photo. So, first of all, can you see the hangar where people were detained at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with number 1. Can you put a number 1 on the hangar that you see?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Next, can you recognise in this photo the place where the -- or the places where the sentry posts were?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sentry posts in the Susica camp were here --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, if you can mark it with number 2.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the guards' hut number 2. And then the entrance gate. Then the corner that was used for toilet purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I see that you made a marking, that you put a number 3; right? Can you tell us what you indicated with number 3?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3 are the sentry posts around the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And can you also see if the place where the women were detained is shown on the photo? And please wait for my instruction before putting any markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. D'Ascoli, I'm a bit confused. I see now two markings by the number 2, and one by the number 3. And the witness just told us that 3 are the sentry posts, in the plural. Now, could we go through it. The number 2 you marked directly under number 1, which is the left of the two 2s you marked, what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the guards' hut where the guards sat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have another marking to the right of that, close to what appears on the picture to be a road which goes from the bottom up. That 2 marks what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second number 2 is the other sentry post by the gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then now you marked 3 as well. What do we -- what did you mark with the 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the third sentry point at the corner, the corner that was used as a toilet and also where the fire hydrant was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear now. Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So we left off -- I was asking whether you can also see the place where women were detained at Susica in this photo.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you place a number 4 on -- on this hangar?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, finally, can you also see the town of Vlasenica in this photo?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The town of Vlasenica can be seen at the top of this page, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If you can mark with number 5, the area where you see Vlasenica town.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you estimate what was the distance between Vlasenica town and the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camp is about 1 kilometre from Vlasenica and about 200 metres away from the first houses of Susica.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this exhibit as marked by the witness. This is P183 already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it needs a new number because of the markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document P183, as marked by the witness, becomes Exhibit P211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed. And well, it's now for -- that was your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Your Honours. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to ask the usher to help us give the witness the statement in B/C/S that was also used by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P207, Your Honours, for identification. That's the statement that this witness gave on the 10th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you, Mr. Osmanovic, to make a short pause between question and answer, and Mr. Stojanovic also will make a brief pause between answer and question, and that is to enable the interpreters to do their job. Mr. Stojanovic, who cross-examines you, is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours .

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Miodrag Stojanovic. We'll try to speak a bit slower, both you and I. It is my understanding on the basis of what you have been saying that up until the beginning of the war there was not a single facility of the JNA in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no garrison of the JNA in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, would you please tell the Trial Chamber where the closest facility of the JNA was before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Han Pijesak, military post code 1524.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Having read your various previous statements about what happened in Vlasenica, it was my understanding that it was on the 21st of April, 1992, that the JNA unit that came from Sekovici entered Vlasenica. To the best of your recollection, could you tell me whether this date is correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 21st and the 23rd. So it's either the 21st, the 22nd, or the 23rd. That's the date when Vlasenica was occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us why you said that on that day - the 21st or the 22nd or the 23rd - Vlasenica was occupied?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the JNA entered Vlasenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So let me just repeat the question. Why did you say that when the JNA entered Vlasenica between the 21st and 23rd of April, 1992, why you did call it an occupation?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called it an occupation for the following reason. As the unit of the JNA entered Vlasenica, Mr. Stojanovic, all the vital functions of town were taken over. Only one ethnic community was armed. Others surrendered their weapons. A curfew was in point. This is classical occupation. One could not leave town. One could not travel freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that already during those days in April 1992 there was the Yugoslavia People's Army, the JNA, and there was the state of Yugoslavia. It was still in existence. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state by way of the referendum; that is to say, that the JNA used to be the joint army but only Serbs stayed in that army. And the army was withdrawing towards the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or, rather, Serbia and Montenegro in the previous period. However, when Vlasenica was occupied, only one ethnic community was armed. Others were not allowed to move about. This is occupation. This is a ghetto.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the time, were you politically involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never politically involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am moving a bit slower so that we could have everything done properly. This is what I'd like to ask you now: After the first multi-party elections in Vlasenica, in that year, 1992, who was in power in the town of Vlasenica itself?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, during the first multi-party elections in Vlasenica, there were two political parties that were struggling for power, the SDS and the SDA. The SDA was given the post of chief of the police administration and the head of the municipality; whereas, the SDS got the commander of the police station, also the head of the executive of the municipality, and also the top posts in various companies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that until the outbreak of the war in 1992, there was practically power-sharing between the two national parties, the SDS and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In April, the population started leaving Vlasenica, both Serbs and Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of April 1992, when the notorious kiss of the lady took place in Bijeljina, when Arkan came from Serbia to calm the situation down in Bosnia, Fikret Abdic and Biljana Plavsic were in Bijeljina as a delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina to thank Arkan for calming things down and stopping a war. However, in Zvornik a conflict broke out and some people from Zvornik went via Vlasenica to Kladanj. Also, conflicts broke out in Bratunac, Bratunac was occupied. Also Vlasenica was occupied. So the ring was closed, if you will. You could only travel towards Han Pijesak where the population is 90 per cent Serb. You could travel in the direction of Sekovici, 97 per cent Serb population. There's only one Muslim village. And you could travel in the direction of Serbia. Ethnic Serbs, namely women and children who were ethnic Serbs, started going to Serbia. We stayed there. They returned once Vlasenica was occupied. However, we stayed on in a ghetto. Mr. Stojanovic, we could not leave without a special pass. This special pass --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you please repeat what you said because your microphone was not activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going ask you about that in relations to the passes. You spoke about that during your examination-in-chief, and I would kindly ask you to focus on the question that I put. Also, would you agree with me that you noticed the Serb population moving from Kladanj towards the territory of Serbia in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard and saw a certain number of women and children at the bus station in Vlasenica. They said that they came from Kladanj and that they were on their way to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the most prominent leader of the Serb people in the area of Vlasenica at that point in time was Mr. Stanic, and Mr. Redzic was the most prominent leader of the Bosniak or Muslim people. Do these two names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Mr. Stanic very well. Also Mr. Redzic. Both of them came to the positions they held in the municipality after the multi-party elections took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, and did you receive any information to this effect, namely, that these two men as leaders of political parties that participate in government in Vlasenica went to Tuzla at one point in time calling upon the people of Vlasenica to return?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the two of them went to Tuzla, but I know that they did say through the media that they were calling upon the people who went to Tuzla to return and that, otherwise, they would lose their property and their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a proclamation that was signed by the leaders of both the Bosniak, that is to say, Muslim party, the SDA, and the Serb party, the SDS?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that on television, Mr. Stojanovic. Now, who signed this, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you heard this proclamation, could you conclude on that basis that the aim was to continue living together in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, I stayed in Vlasenica, but I could not come to the conclusion that that was a life together in co-existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The political leadership of the Muslim people had already left Vlasenica by the 21st of April. They went towards Tuzla and Kladanj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The unit of the JNA that on the 21st, or up to the 23rd at any rate, came from Sekovici. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the direction of Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, as you say in your statement - not to look at it now, you will remember that - to the best of your recollection, it was headed by a young man, a lieutenant, an ethnic Albanian; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard this from a young soldier whose accent was from Sandzak. He told me that his commander was Lieutenant Musa. Musa could not be a Serb. Musa was an Albanian and he was in charge of that unit. This young soldier was a regular soldier of the JNA, passing through Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that in April 1992 the decision had already been passed to declare Bosnia-Herzegovina an independent state?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you know from Vlasenica, was that in accordance with the will of the Serb people or, rather, your neighbours that you talked to and were in communication with?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs had a plebescite; the Muslims had a referendum. The Serbs were in favour of staying in Yugoslavia and that was demonstrated in the plebescite and the Muslims, or, rather, all the rest were in favour of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this was a period during which two constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina had totally opposed opinions about the state they wanted to live in?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had two completely opposed positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now have a look at paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is in the witness's statement, P207 is the number. We were mentioning Lieutenant Musa earlier on. Let's have a look at paragraph 6. We'll have a look at part of your statement, the part where you say that the JNA started -- I'll just wait for it to turn up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, halfway down the paragraph: "The JNA started informing the people to surrender all their weapons. I did not see any Muslims in that JNA unit, only Serbs." Can you see that part? A little earlier you said according to the information you had an Albanian was the officer in charge of that unit. What I'm interested in is how it is that you know that there were no members of other ethnic groups, so only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, out of the people I recognised in those groups, and I'm referring to my neighbours, my Serb neighbours, among them I didn't see a single Muslim from Vlasenica. Those people who came from other parts weren't familiar with the town. They didn't know where there were more Muslim houses and where there were fewer Serbian ones. This is why I said that I did not see a single Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But can we agree that you do not know what ethnicity the members of that JNA unit were, that unit that came to your place from some other direction?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you can't exclude the possibility that at that point in time that unit, and an Albanian was in charge of it, as you said, you can't exclude the possibility that there were perhaps members in that unit of a different ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exclude that possibility, but of the people I knew their ethnicity was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll deal with that later. You served in the JNA from 1984 to 1985; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Niksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were in Niksic in a unit that was a reconnaissance unit. That's where you were trained?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the reconnaissance unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who your officer was?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Smajlovic, Shefkija [phoen] was my officer. Lieutenant Radenko Tomovic, and Kosovac Boskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the JNA in 1985, seven years prior to the events, was a multi-ethnic body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is there any dispute between the parties that the 1985 the JNA was a multi-ethnic armed force? Is there any dispute about it? I'm asking this question because apart from matters not being in dispute to be avoided in the examination of a witness, also the level of relevance of most of what you have dealt with until now is rather unclear -- no, it's -- it is clear to us that the level of relevance is low, very low. Could you please start focussing on matters that are in dispute and are of a high level of relevance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour. I'm moving in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Having served in the army, I assume that you reported to the Ministry of Defence in Vlasenica and you were given a war-time assignment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in accordance with that war-time assignment, you were issued with appeals for training sessions or mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of such a unit. My assignment was in the fire brigade in Vlasenica because I had joined the fire brigade as a child, I had passed the exams, so my war-time assignment had to do with the volunteer fire brigade in Vlasenica and I was a non-commissioned officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this question for the following reason. At the time, the first half of 1992, if you had received a call-up to report to a JNA unit, would you have reported to such a unit?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because, Mr. Stojanovic, my father was a member of the JNA. He worked, he was employed by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would your fellow Muslim citizens at the time in 1992, would they have responded to a JNA -- the JNA call-up? Did they respond to the JNA call-up?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I can only speak for myself. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that the general position was that it wasn't good respond to the call-up and go to the JNA, that was the Muslim position in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would you agree that that is correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, some military documents were taken in Vlasenica. The SDA prohibited those documents, those military documents from being taken away. Or, rather, there were demonstrations, peaceful demonstrations. As to whether someone responded the call-up, I don't know. Did anyone summon anyone to join up? I don't know. But I know that I myself, given my position, given my attitude, I know that I would have responded to that call-up, to such a call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it is in that context that I want to conclude my questions about this area. In April 1992, the reason for which there were no Muslims in the reserve and regular JNA force was the fact that the JNA didn't want to join those units, didn't want to respond to the call-ups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you have such information. I didn't have any such information, so I can't say whether that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Muslims did not want to respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at paragraph 6 again. You say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, P207, paragraph 6 is what we are looking in the following sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say: "After the weapons had been collected, Serb shops and bars began to open." Can you see that part?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what sort of weapons were collected by the JNA and from whom?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, Your Honours, the weapons were collected from people of Muslim ethnicity. The JNA was looking for legal and illegal weapons. They wanted such weapons to be surrendered at the time. I know that the legal weapons people had were hunting rifles, sports weapons, and pistols. As for rifles and automatic weapons, it wasn't possible to legally to have such weapons. Neither side could legally have such weapons, the Serbs, the Muslims, or anyone else. The Territorial Defence had such weapons, as well as the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know - because this is what you say in your statement - do you know what sort of weapons were involved after they had been collected? What sort of weapons did the JNA collect?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, they were looking for legal and illegally possessed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say they collected illegal weapons, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said legal and illegal weapons. Both types of weapons. Illegal weapons are all weapons that you possess without a permit issued by the public security station in Vlasenica. In fact, this was done through the court. And let me just add something else, Mr. Stojanovic. While television Novi Sad was operational there was a broadcast from Vlasenica and they showed a mass of weapons, hunting rifles, carbines - that's a hunting weapon - and they showed two automatic weapons and one Skorpion, and they said that these were weapons that had been prepared to kill Serbs with. The Novi Sad television showed that in April 1992, broadcast this in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about this. Sir, do you know from which part of Vlasenica municipality these weapons were collected?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which part of Vlasenica they were collected in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And given what you said, when they asked -- when they were looking for weapons, do you know whether the SDA did issue weapons in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard about that, but I never saw such things myself. Because as I wasn't a member of the party, nor was anyone else from my family a member of that party, even if there was such information, it would have been concealed from me. I'd only like to add one other thing, Mr. Stojanovic. I socialised with a Serb. We were very good friends. So if they had had anything, they would have concealed this from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now have a look at paragraph 28 in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 28, Your Honours, in the B/C/S and in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to turn up on the screen, Mr. Osmanovic, we were taking about the events concerning the part of Vlasenica called Drum. Would you, first of all, tell the Court where that part of Vlasenica municipality is located, where Drum is located.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drum is 1 kilometre from Vlasenica, Your Honours. It's behind the "boksit" sports stadium or, rather, it's behind the Muslim cemetery called Rakite. There were two Serbian houses in that village. All the other houses were Muslim. Piskavice, Dzamdzici, and Bare were the other villages in the vicinity, and then the municipality extended in the direction of other villages. So that is the closest suburb to Vlasenica. The suburb that is closest to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, this area was inhabited by Muslims almost exclusively?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were only two Serbian families there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Somewhere in the middle of your statement, you say that at the beginning of the conflict in Bijeljina, before the JNA arrived Vlasenica, at the cross-roads where the road leads to Drum, there was a Muslim check-point.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this information you personally had?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You forgot to switch on your microphone with your previous question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat the question for the sake of the transcript. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, my question was as follows. I was quoting your words. As you said, at the cross-roads where the road leads to Drum, there was a Muslim check-point. And my question is whether you had direct information on the existence of this check-point?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you personally see? What sort of a check-point was it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were young men who lived in Drum there, and they would not allow certain individuals whom they did not know to pass through, because they knew who lived in Piskavice, Drum, Zekici, Pusumac [phoen]. The people who lived in those areas, Serbs and Muslims, could pass through without hindrance, but those who were not local inhabitants could not pass through. They were not armed but they did not let them pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say this was sometime around the beginning of the conflict in Bijeljina. To the best of your recollection, since I am from Bijeljina, I'd like to ask you when this conflict in Bijeljina took place?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the beginning of April, Mr. Stojanovic, at the time of Ramadan and after Ramadan in 1992. The conflict in Bijeljina started when Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, arrived. Television footage has been shown about this event --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I'd like to confer with my client for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you heard what we were saying, but we have to confirm that the events in Bijeljina occurred, as you say, at the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't want to mix this up with the time of the religious festival. It's for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, this having been clarified, whether you come from Bijeljina or from whatever other place is irrelevant and should not be included in your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will bear that in mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that that check-point was just before the Drum settlement, you're not referring to the road. You're referring to a part of the place of Vlasenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Drum in Turkish means "road," but it doesn't mean "road." I wasn't referring to a road, I was referring to the settlement. It was about 200 metres away at a cross-roads where the road forks off for Drum and for the village of Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How is it possible that in that period, that is to say, the beginning of April 1992, someone, and, as you say, he is a civilian, takes over the authority of the state and allows someone to go down that part of the road?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, someone gave himself the right to place a check-point at Drum and also at Tisca. I saw that when I came from Sarajevo, or, rather, from Breza. When the police brought me from Kladanj to Vlasenica; that is to say, myself and the young men who were at the police school in Vrace. I arrived together with them, and at Tisca I saw a check-point that was held by the Serbs who were armed, whereas in Drum there were two people -- there were people in two vehicles. I did not see any weapons, though. Who allowed both of them to do this, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, if I understand you correctly, in view of your own position, your own views, you never supported either one of the check-points that you came across.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not support either one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you would agree that it is precisely that kind of thing that turned certain parts of the municipality of Vlasenica into a ghetto, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Acts like that contributed to a rise in tensions and even more intolerance. A ghetto, as I've already said. Regrettably, I stayed on there and I lived there together with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because of the following sentence in your statement. Could you please explain that to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- so, Your Honour, paragraph 28. It's where this -- this witness's statement continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you say this and you can see this, Mr. Osmanovic. "I think that at the beginning of the conflict the village of Drum was better organised than the Muslims in Vlasenica."

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were you trying to say when you stated that the village of Drum was better organised?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least they knew who was coming to their village. Who was coming, who was passing there. Whoever wanted to came to Vlasenica and they did whatever they wanted to do. Mr. Stojanovic, when the war started in 1992, a vast number of people all of a sudden showed up in military uniforms with weapons at the hotel there in Vlasenica, the Panorama Hotel; that is to say, before the JNA arrived. For that reason, I'm trying to say that they were much better organised than others because they knew who was coming and who was passing there. They did not forbid ethnic Serbs and Muslims to go do their homes, but they did not allow people from other areas to stay in their village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of what you've said just now, and you believe that to be the position of the residents of Drum, what would have happened if that JNA unit passed down that road?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA unit did come down that road with an APC, and they parked it in a Muslim cemetery there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed at any point in time that there was any kind of shooting from that part of Vlasenica or from the village of Drum? That there was any shooting at the JNA units.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been informed of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed that precisely from that area, from Drum, weapons had been taken, those that had been distributed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the army asked for weapons to be surrendered, legal and illegal weapons, that pertained to the village of Drum and the village of Piskavice and the neighbourhood and the town of Vlasenica. So it referred to the town and the outskirts. The only part of the municipality of Vlasenica that did not respond to that was the local commune of Cerska. They did not abide by that all the way up until February 1993. They were totally encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now you are leading me to ask this question. You say that Cerska was totally encircled?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And if I were to put it to you that Cerska was part of the corridor where the population and the army moved all the way up until March 1993 from Srebrenica, Pobudje, Konjevic Polje, Cerska, Snagovo, Sapna, Godus, and Tuzla, would I be right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cerska was a territory -- I mean, my father hails from Cerska. My mother had been expelled from Vlasenica to Cerska. My sister was in Cerska. They were there until February 1993. From there, they passed through Maricici, Snagovo, Liplje, Kamenica, Jasenica, to the area of Medjedja, rather the municipality of Sapna, and they arrived Tuzla. The others, the remainder of the population went to Srebrenica. So Cerska was empty, it remained empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So would we agree in view of the locations that you spoke about, that it was only in February or March 1993 that Cerska came under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March. Or in February, because my family members left in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more sentence before the break, or, rather, one question. You heard of the killing of reserve Captain Savo Bacic in Begici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Bacic personally and I did not hear of his killing. Savo Bacic was a reserve captain first class and he worked in the Territorial Defence Staff of the municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed that in that period, in April 1992, the village of Pepic between Kladanj, Sekovici, and Vlasenica had been torched?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not been informed about that, although I know where the village is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Stojanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I'm now going to move onto a different topic, perhaps this would be the right moment to take a break, Your Honours. With your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the right time to take a break. First, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we take a break, the Chamber thought that the core of the testimony of this witness was about what he experienced in the camps, in prisons, about what was done to those persons. It seems that you're not challenging, in any way, what happened there. Is that what -- is that well understood? Because we hear a lot about background events. May I -- it's not quite clear to the Chamber yet whether that would explain why people behaved as they did or whether that would justify what the behaviour of what -- of those who acted in the camps and the prisons. It's not clear to the Chamber. But we noticed that it's all about background and nothing about the core of the testimony of this witness, as we find it in his statement. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And with your leave, I have hereby concluded the background part of the examination of this witness. Now we are going to deal with all the three -- the detention centres where he was. We'd just like to clarify certain questions that he had raised. We're not going to be dealing with background any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I then take it that you will be able to conclude that within one hour. Is that well understood? Because we now know the name of the commander of the unit under which the witness served when he was in the JNA. The Chamber doesn't know what to do with that information, but at least we now know it. Relevance of it is very low. I earlier indicated that we would expect you to focus on more relevant issues. You said you would come to that. The Chamber wonders whether you actually did or not. You have one hour after the break, and please focus on relevant issues, relevant issues that are in dispute between the parties. We take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we continue, Mr. Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 20 of your statement, 2-0, P207. I have a question -- a few questions about this statement. But first of all, would I be right in saying that on 22 July 1993, you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, you gave several statements to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You gave statements on the 23rd, two days after you were released, or, rather, exchanged to the security organ of the 2nd Corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian army in Lukavac. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that various security agencies came and rallied us together and took statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your next statement was given on the 27th July, and another one on the 4th of August 1993; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the dates, but I know that they did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We will show them. I only wanted to get authorisation. So in paragraph 20 you describe at length your experience and the -- your presence at the murder of Mr. Ambeskovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the last few sentences in that paragraph. You say, after describing the shot: "During this incident, there were no other shadows in the door. I heard no other voices or anyone approaching the door. When Mumovic opened the door, he appeared to be alone. I believe Mumovic acted alone, as the incident took place very quickly." Now I'm asking you: Do you still stand by your assertion that this incident at the time when you were detained in Vlasenica happened in the way you described in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave this statement to The Hague Tribunal. It is a very thorough statement. We went over every segment chronologically, and I do stand behind this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this for the following reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 1D260, Your Honours, and focus on the central part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You will now see, Mr. Osmanovic, it is your statement given on the 4th of the August, 1983 [as interpreted], to the War Crimes Bureau in Lukavac. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you misspeak or is there just an error in the transcription. It must be 1993, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I thought I said 1993, but maybe I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to the next page in English so that the Court can follow, and stay with this current page in the B/C/S. We should focus on the last few lines in B/C/S which correspond to this paragraph in the English version we see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, concerning the same incident, you say on the 4th of August, 1993, after being exchanged, the following: Among other things, you say that Mr. Ambeskovic, who was a retired public security officer in Zvornik, succumbed to Chetnik torture and beating by Zoran Viskovic, also known as Vjetar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This copy is very bad, I mean the B/C/S one. So I can't see what is written and I don't understand English. Dzemal Ambeskovic, a retired policeman, traffic policeman from Zvornik, son of Kadro, and mother Tamila, was politically involved man in the preparation of the referendum for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. Zoran Viskovic beat him - and it's true that he beat him - and as you say, he succumbed -- he succumbed in the same police station when Stevo Mumovic -- that man would have died any way. He was too badly beaten up. But since I can't read the B/C/S here, I stand by my statement that it was Stevo Mumovic who deprived Mr. Ambeskovic of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: With your leave, could we just enlarge the last four lines in the B/C/S version because it is successfully translated into English. I will read it and you can follow. It says that you stated and signed that Mr. Ambeskovic succumbed - you can follow the text - to Chetnik torture and beating by Zoran Viskovic. Therefore, my question: Which of your two statements would be true today?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that Dzemal Ambeskovic was killed by a bullet. As to the beating, he was already in great distress and suffering from the beating. Zoran Viskovic beat him the most badly. He simply tortured him beyond any reason. Ambeskovic had once released to go home, but he got lost around the village of Turalici and went back. It was his last trip. He was my good neighbour. When he was released from the police station, he was so black and blue, covered in bruises and lesions. There was just one fence between us. I -- I doubt that the man could have survived this beating even if he had not stayed in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's try to move on more quickly. So it's not true that he was killed by the beating from Zoran Viskovic. He was killed by the shot fired by Stevo Mumovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what finally killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see P207 again in e-court, please. Paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this to be uploaded, could we agree that, on the 22nd May 1992, you were arrested for the first time? You were arrested by policemen from the police station in Vlasenica; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them were active-duty policemen, Mr. Stojanovic. Two of them wore reserve police uniforms. Those were blue. One had a camouflage uniform. But they were armed and they belonged to that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to clear up. Now look, in this paragraph 17 of your statement - we'll do this very quickly. You say that Bastah, Rade Milic, and in proofing you changed this name to identify Deuric Zoran, son of Zoran.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The information about Rade Milic is something you did not mention in your earlier statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention Rade Milic because that man acted as a professional towards all of his neighbours. His brother lived across the street from me. The man was very professional. I had no reason to identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So in your earlier statements, where you described this event, you did not provide full information. Instead, you said it was an unidentified uniformed member of the police.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I said even here that I saw in the car a man I didn't know aged around 30. Later, I found out his name was Rajkenovic [phoen]. They came for me in a police car.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And they took you to the police station where you spent the time from 22nd May to 2nd June, when you were transferred to the municipal prison. You spent 17 days there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was transferred to Susica camp on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have a misunderstanding about that too, but before that let me ask you: You were moved to the municipal prison at the intercession of Boro Mijic, a Serb from Vlasenica who knew you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the active-duty policemen in Vlasenica knew me because the fire brigade, of which I was a member, and the police station were in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The conditions in the municipal prison were fair and more decent than in the previous prison?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Especially when Mr. Sokanovic visited who introduced himself of the warden of the prison. In his presence we were treated correctly. We were able to go to the toilet. We could air the cells. We could receive food brought to us from home. But without him, it was all a lottery. It depended on whether somebody dared to do something or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were told that you were being investigated for possession of weapons or any other reason for being on that list you had seen in the hands of your friend?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it because a friend showed it to me. I was never questioned about the circumstances that could have led to my name being included on that list. I wasn't told anything. And when we were moved to the municipal prison, we had gotten out of the hell of the police station. We had better capability of receiving food from home, and sometimes we would go out to do some loading or unloading and be there at the looting of Bosniak houses and property, where we also got some food.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you did have information that, under some circumstances unknown to you, and by people also unknown to you, you were put on that list under number 194 as a person who was in illegal possession of weapons.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody must have reported me, but I really never had any weapons, especially not illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I've move to the next area. You mentioned two names. Mr. Mumovic, was he a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Mumovic was born in born in Ricica village, Han Pijesak municipality, before the war. He had served a sentence in the prison of Foca. He had killed a man, Ferid Bemic, by cutting him with a knife. And before the war started, he showed up in uniform with the emblem that said "war-time police."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please leave a pause between question and answer and repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Could you repeat your question. And the interpreters invite you to make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat my question for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Viskovic belong to the same police force, the one you mentioned also?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Viskovic was an employee of a trade company, Polet. He wore a uniform and he was in the police station until 1990 -- in 1992. Until 1992, he had worked in this company, Polet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So would I be right in saying that you were driven in a police car by policemen wearing uniforms to the police station in Vlasenica. Then you spent some time there. You were moved to the municipal prison, and there the policemen guarded you.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 18th of June, 1992, you were moved to Susica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clear up this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 1D260 in e-court. It's the statement we had just looked at. Page 2. And page 2 in English. In fact, we need page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, you say, if can you find the place, it's paragraph 4, you say that on the 19th of June, 1992, we were transferred with 11 or 12 people to the Susica camp. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that on the 18th or 19th, well, give or take a day, it didn't matter whether I was in Susica or in the prison at the time, but we were transferred in Dragan Bastah's lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to know what date you think it is now.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th. Because later I obtained other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'd like to deal with what happened in the Susica centre. Do you remember that you spoke about the prisoner Handzic from Ledici being killed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said -- we can follow this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have a look at paragraph 38 in P207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see that Dragan Nikolic was responsible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Nikolic, also known as Jenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 33 you describe the abuse of Mr. Reuf Rasidagic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the mid-part of that statement you say that you saw Nikolic beating Reuf. "Reuf was close to me in the hangar. Only Nikolic beat him."

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So to deal with this, let's now have a look at paragraph 42 in the very same statement. And in that paragraph, you again describe everything that you witnessed in Susica. You say with regard to the abuse that Galib Smajlovic and Dzevad Saric were subjected to -- can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that they were beaten or, rather, taken out by Ljubinko Djuric, Nikolic, Ljubisa Vukotic, and Sinisa Orasanin. Could you now tell the Court whether Mr. Dzevad Saric succumbed to the wounds inflicted in this beating?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he had been beaten, Dzevad Saric was returned to the hangar, as well as Galib Smajlovic. Galib Smajlovic was shaking as a result of the beating. Meho Kuljancic put salt dressings on Dzevad's wounds -- on Galib's wounds, but Dzevad was taken out with Kozarovic Muharem on the same evening, and also with Zekic and Perhad [phoen] Begovic. They were taken outside and after the beating he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to deal with an inconsistency here. Could we now have a look at 1D261. Transcript 1D261. We've checked this in the database. We don't have an English version but I'll do my best. I will only read out one sentence. And we will have the B/C/S version. Sir, it says the 27th of July, 1993. And that's the date on which you gave the State Security Service in Tuzla this statement. Do you remember giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at page 2, please. I apologise. Page 3. We can both have a look at it now. It's halfway down the page. You describe the event in question and you say the following: "The following night Nikolic beat Smajlovic, Galib and Savic, Dzevad, who succumbed to the beatings." Would you agree with me that this does not tally with what you said in your statement in paragraph 42? It's not consistent with what you said there.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what is at stake here is the following. When they were taken out that evening, no shots could be heard. Only at the end. But you could only hear screams. On that evening, I was taken out. Unfortunately I raised my head when they were taking them out and Zoran Obrenovic and Sladjan Pajic asked me who tried to flee. As I said, I was sleeping. Dubenko [phoen] Djuric stood by my side and by my brother's side. They took out Rasid Ferhatbegovic from Papraca, and that evening only one shot could be heard. So he could have died only as a result of the beating or because a knife had been used. Bullets -- or a bullet was not used in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you about is the following. Having considered everything you said in paragraphs 42 and 44 of your statement, P207, what I would like to know is what is in fact is correct. Who was abusing him at the time that he succumbed to his wounds?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he succumbed to his wounds, Dubenko Djuric, Zoran Obrenovic, Sladjan Pajic, son of Radislav, with a -- Zoran Obrenovic, son of Vojo and Dragica was there. Those are the people I saw that evening when those four individuals succumbed to the wounds inflicted on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you've asked the questions to the witness. Could you tell me, because I have no English version of your -- the statement you just used, exactly where the inconsistency is found? What exactly is different? Again, I can't re-read it, so -- I mean, you've asked the witness, so therefore I'm seeking clarification so as to better understand both your question and the answer the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question will be quite concise now. Your Honours will remove the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement of the 27th of July that I read out to you, you said on the following evening Nikolic beat Smajlovic and Saric, Dzevad who succumbed to the blows, with your leave. And in the statement that you have given again today, you mentioned certain other names, names of individuals who took Mr. Saric out, and you say they subjected him to abuse. So my question was: What is, in fact, correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have been given the answer, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My problem is not, Mr. Stojanovic, to ask the witness again. But where exactly the inconsistency is. I mean, is beating someone excludeing that that person was taken out, or -- I do not see exactly - also because I can't re-read it - where exactly the inconsistency is and what it exactly is. Is it that you say you can't be beaten if you are taken out or is it that you say it is the persons or -- what exactly is the inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to testify, but the inconsistency has to do with the identity of the person who took Saric outside and inflicted wounds on him. So that's why I wanted to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you have been provided with the answer, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the transcript, I'd like to repeat that the correct answer would be that he was taken out by the individuals you mentioned in paragraph 42 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now move on and try and clear up certain other issues, certain other inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. I really still don't understand. In paragraph 42 of the statement, P207, in the fourth line, I see the name Nikolic there. In the sentence: "They were taken out by Ljubinko Djuric," then the next name is Nikolic, and then Ljubisa Vukotic. I see the name Nikolic. Where is the inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Nikolic. Your Honours, I'll just repeat a sentence from the statement that he provided on the 27th of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explained to me, Mr. Stojanovic, that the inconsistency was in the persons who had taken this man out. Now, you read to us and you drew our attention to the two statements. You asked the witness whether he remembered that he had given a statement. Then you said, have a look at page 2, and you read to him the following: "The following night Nikolic beat Smajlovic, Galib and Savic, Dzevad, who succumbed to the beatings." That line you read doesn't say a word about who took him out. So, therefore, if you say the inconsistency is that in the one statement another person took this man out, then at least in the second one there is not a word about who took him out. Only about who had beaten him. So therefore it's still, even after your explanation, it is not clear to me where now exactly the inconsistency is. Not in the taking out, because the second statement, the old statement, doesn't say anything about it. Or it does, but we can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, because I also mentioned paragraph 44. Could we have a look at P207 on the screen. I think it will then be quite clear why I wanted to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before we do that, Mr. Stojanovic, did I understand you well that you explained the inconsistency to be in the person that had taken the man out? I think that's what you said. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours. That's the first inconsistency that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no. I -- just wait for a second. Do you also agree with me that the line that you read to the witness, which is the only line this Chamber has heard because we have no English translation, doesn't say a word about who took a person, the persons, out?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's also correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there can be no inconsistency in this respect and your explanation is unsatisfactory. And you should, on the basis of what you tell us now, not have put to the witness that there is an inconsistency. Now if you want to further look at his statement, that's fine. But I just focussed on what was unclear to me until now. I asked you for an explanation. That explanation is - I think we agree on that - is not valid. So please proceed, and refrain at least on this basis, putting to the witness that there is an inconsistency. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll return to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To paragraphs 42 and 44 in your statement, Mr. Osmanovic, and I think that we will try and deal with this contradiction. You say that: "Ljubinko, Djuric, Nikolic, Ljubisa Vukotic, and Sinisa Orasanin, and then some other guards took them out. All I could here were the screams. Their screaming." And then in paragraph 44 you -- you add that when they returned Saric, and at one point in time the same guards went in, woke Saric up. Obrenovic then told Saric to go outside. As soon as the door closed, I heard a terrible scream. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the last part of paragraph 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So my question is: Can you today tell us whether what you said on the 27th is correct, what you said in the statement I have quoted from? And in that statement you say that Nikolic beat Saric up and Saric succumbed to the blows.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Galib Smajlovic and Dzevad Saric were beaten by Nikolic, Mr. Stojanovic. Dzevad Saric was black and blue. He was black and blue. When this other group of guards came, and that's what I referred to in paragraph 44, when they came and took him outside, all you could hear was this terrible screaming, a scream, the kind of which you can only hear in horror films. Dzevad Saric never returned to the hangar in the camp again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot say whether he succumbed to the wounds that were inflicted by Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the wounds were in the form of hematoma.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the management structure of Susica, Veljko Basic, in your view, was the warden of Susica; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman, right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a retired policeman of the public security station of Vlasenica who was reactivated in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of security was the mentioned Dragan Nikolic, a member of the special police unit that was under the commander of Mico Kraljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic, nicknamed Jenki, introduced him as the commander, as God All Mighty, as the Alpha and Omega of the prison, and that he had only one commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Susica - and that was those 12 days, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 18th or 19th until the 30th of the June. Was it your understanding that the facility was under the control of the police in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, since this facility was frequented by one and all, whenever anybody felt like it, people who had weapons, this was under the command of Dragan Nikolic, Jenki, but there was also people in uniform, in S and B uniforms who came there, and who, during the course of the day, took a group of people out to work in the garrison that was established in the old high school in Vlasenica. Also people who were in camouflage uniforms came. They came to work on cleaning the town. Also people who wore dark blue uniforms came. No regular policemen ever came there, people who had been employed at the regular police station before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I have the same question for the inconsistency between 42 and 44. You've asked the witness about it. Tell us exactly where the inconsistency is found, to better understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, in the statement that was admitted into evidence as P207, in paragraphs 42 and 44, the witness mentioned the names of four persons, including a man with the last name of Nikolic who took Mr. Saric out. That's paragraph 42. And after they took him out, this witness said that he only heard screams. In paragraph 44, this witness says - and he stood by that when answering my questions today - that these very same guards went in again, woke up Saric, and now he adds another name of a name who has -- a person who has the last name of Obrenovic. And this same Obrenovic said to Saric to go out. Your Honour, in the statement that I quoted - and, unfortunately, I don't have the English version - and that's perhaps at the core of this misunderstanding that I've caused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. First of all, you suggested that there was an inconsistency between paragraph 42 and 44, but I now do understand that these paragraphs are inconsistent with the other statement. Now, again, that other statement, the part you read to us, was not saying anything about who took out who at what point in time from where. If there is any portion you would like to address in this respect, I would invite you to read that part of the statement which is then inconsistent with paragraphs 42 and 44. You may have noticed that 42 and 44, that 42 describes what happened on the 25th, and that, at that moment, the person taken -- persons taken out were -- were returning. And then what is described in paragraph 44 is what happened on the 26th of June. So, therefore, it is a -- there are two occasions where Mr. Saric apparently was taken out. But now give us the line or the portion of the statement dealing with who took out Mr. Saric. And then, of course, we are interested also to know when, but ... tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try, Your Honour. If I may, I'll just repeat the part that is of interest to me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, please follow what I'm saying. He says here: "During the course of the night" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you are at this moment informing the Chamber. You are not questioning, you're not examining the witness. The Chamber asked clarification. Read to us the lines which, in your view, create the inconsistency. The previous line did not; we agreed on that. Now please read the line which is inconsistent with what is found in 42 and 44. And tell the interpreters and also us where approximately we find it in this B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe could we have 1D261 on the screens, because I still see the statement P207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We now move to -- to the document which is only available in B/C/S. Please read it, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just read that sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, what is page 3 in e-court is, at least in my version, not what appears on our screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then where? Page 3, in my e-court version, starts with the date 30.06.1992. Apparently I'm looking at a different page 3... okay. Let's -- yes, I look at the other screen. Where now do we find it, what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely where the cursor is now, where it says: "The next night, Nikolic beat up Galib Smajlovic and Dzevad Saric who succumbed to the blows." So in the statement that the witness gave and that was admitted into evidence in this case, there is no mention of Nikolic being the person who inflicted the blows on him that -- the ones that he succumbed to. Also on the basis of Mr. Nikolic's plea agreement, I would like to ask the witness to tell us what it is that is actually correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. You earlier said: So now it is not who took him out but apparently who inflicted blows. And the -- let me just see. Where do we know exactly which date we are talking about? Because I see the 19th of June at the beginning of this paragraph. And you said the next evening. I also see the 30th of June, 1992. But what the next evening is is unclear to me when I'm not able to read this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
